subject: EX-20-004
comment: I would like to appose the exemption being requested. The previous owners of property in question purposefully built an "add-on" to their home with the full intent to use this add-on as an unapproved duplex. These past owners where happy to share this information with neighbors, and thought themselves quite clever. When the property recently came up for sale, the relator was also letting everyone who called know that this was an ILLEGAL duplex. My wife and I called the relator, interested in the sale price, and where told this information before anything else. The new owners of this property where surely also warned about the illegal nature of the property, and choose buy the property with full intent to continue to rent. If you approve this exemption this sets a VERY bad precedent for the community, one where the rules and regulations of the City are blatantly ignored and then manipulated after the fact at the expense of the neighborhood. Duplexes in this area with the current zoning are intended for 2 family units. Instead, at least one of the units is consistently sub- let. While sub-leasing is not the topic of discussion, it has historically attracted individuals who do not participate or interact in the community. The number of sub-letters also often increases to more than 4 individuals, which bypasses the permissible amount. The "MillCreek Together General Plan" for the area in question is listed as a "Neighborhood 1." This type of neighborhood is zoned to be predominately single-family homes. This type of unit does not fit with this plan. This plan also calls for 64% single-family homes and a total of 10% town home, condo, or duplex. From the house in question to 45th south- the number of these (non- single-family homes) is approximately 20%, over double the intended amount. For the neighborhood in general there are over 30% of the homes that are duplexes. Allowing an exemption would not enable the city to maintain the goals listed in the General Plan and maintain the neighborhood as a Neighborhood 1. This property sits at the end of a street that connects to a circle. There is insufficient parking provided for the unsanctioned number of people living at this property, there is insufficient parking. Due to the parking on both sides of the entrance to the circle, there is typically room for one vehicle to enter or exit the circle, not both as is intended, at a time. The renters regularly speed around the circle - turning what should be a safe circle into a dangerous area. With the cars regularly parking on the circle "street" and being that the house in question is at the end of the circle- there is often very cramp conditions when entering or exiting the circle. This parking is due to another infraction—each night 2 to 3 vehicles are parked within the 20 feet of the corner of the circle. It is well documented that on-street parking results in decreased visibility to both pedestrians and vehicles. On-street parking accounts for 72% of all accidents on local streets. The regulations in place to reduce this risk are ignored. Even if the current tenants were different, a corner duplex in this type of neighborhood increases the likelihood of on-street parking, directly increasing the risk for an accident. While an unsafe circle on its own is troubling, it is made even worse in our circle due to the waking path that connects the circle to 45th south. This waking path is intended to improve the safety of access to 4500 South, particularly for pedestrian, cyclists, and access to public transportation. As such, it is regularly trafficked by young families, children, the elderly, as well as special needs individuals from our community. The General Plan encourages walkways and safe walking neighborhoods, and having a duplex on the corner of the road leading to one of these walkways significantly increases the risk of a pedestrian-vehicle accident. While the new owner of this property is surely hoping to turn a quick buck, or bring in a little extra money off this rental, the lasting impacts of the property to those who actually live in the community are not justified by their gain. Neighbors have pervasively filed complaints about the illegal nature of the property. Even the nature and timing of this exemption reflects that, targeting a holiday weekend when many in the community are out of town
